paras: The lynching of John Daniels took place in February 1919, when a mob took Daniels, a Black man charged with murder, from the jail at Jacksonville, North Carolina, in Onslow County, and hanged him from the Neuse River bridge. A second prisoner, Daniel Pettaway, was taken with him and was supposed to have been lynched as well. Black newspapers in Cleveland and Wisconsin reported it as another North Carolina lynching, and the Wisconsin Weekly Blade later reprinted a Raleigh editorial deploring it.

Daniels, described as "Colored," was held in the Jacksonville jail charged with the murder of Grover Dickey, manager of a lumber company. Daniel Pettaway was held in the same jail as his accomplice. The Raleigh News and Observer later described the killing that preceded the lynching as one in which "a Negro killed a white man."

According to a dispatch from Newburg dated February 12, the mob took Daniels from the jail "early last Friday," which would be February 7. A brief datelined Jacksonville said he was hanged from the Neuse River bridge. The mob also took Pettaway from the jail; by the time of the dispatch no trace of him had been found, and it was "supposed that he also was lynched." None of the reports gives the size of the mob, names any of its members, or describes what the jailers did.

No report of an inquest, arrests, or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage, and no later report on Pettaway was found. Writing about the case, the Raleigh News and Observer said prosecuting officers ought to identify and punish lynchers but predicted they were "not going to be, as a rule, successful" until public sentiment changed.

The Cleveland Advocate carried the first report found, on February 15, under the headline "North Carolina Stages Anofher Lynching Bee." Three weeks later the Wisconsin Weekly Blade ran a two-sentence item among its national briefs, adding the bridge detail and calling it "the third lynching in this state within the year." Neither item gave the accusation in more than a phrase, and only the Advocate named Dickey or Pettaway.

On April 5 the Blade printed an editorial headed "The Onslow Lynching," credited at its close to the Raleigh News and Observer, a North Carolina paper. The editorial called the lynching "greatly to be regretted" and said the lynching of Negroes was "merely piling up trouble for both races later on." It also held that "a Negro killed a white man bringing on the trouble in Onslow," and described the lynchers as white men who "ought to have had more self-restraint" and committed "a second murder" in the belief that it was justified by the first. By reprinting it, the Blade put before its readers a North Carolina paper's condemnation, which paired regret over the lynching with doubt that the lynchers would be punished.

framing.detail: The Cleveland Advocate's headline, 'North Carolina Stages Anofher Lynching Bee', presented it as one more in a series.
The Wisconsin Weekly Blade ran a two-sentence brief, adding only that it was the state's third lynching within the year.

The Blade reprinted a Raleigh editorial that called the lynching 'greatly to be regretted' and 'a second murder' but placed the start of 'the trouble' on the Negro who killed a white man and doubted lynchers would be punished.
